title: The Disappearance of Memorization -- And What We Lost
author: Ayaan Hirsi Ali
summary: The essay argues that American education has largely abandoned memorization as a serious pedagogical practice, dismissing it as mere 'drudgery' in an age when information is a search away -- and that this abandonment has cost students far more than it saved them. Drawing on Louis Pasteur's dictum that 'chance favors only the prepared mind,' the piece contends that invention, discovery, and even basic reading comprehension depend on a substantial base of internalized factual and linguistic knowledge, citing E.D. Hirsch's argument that broad background knowledge is what makes strong readers and Daniel Willingham's research that critical thinking itself requires extensive factual knowledge to operate on. The author traces the decline back at least to the early 1980s, when memorization was already being dismissed as a 'luxury,' and argues that this was a category error: skills like analysis and critical thinking were falsely set up in opposition to fact-based learning rather than understood as dependent on it. The piece closes by reframing memorization as an act of cultural transmission -- filling students' minds with what is 'worthy of study' so that shared texts and knowledge can elevate a common civic and intellectual life.
points: Uses Louis Pasteur's 'chance favors only the prepared mind' to argue that what looks like effortless genius or insight actually depends on internalized prior knowledge built through memorization.

Cites E.D. Hirsch's claim that broad knowledge acquisition is precisely what makes a good reader, tying memorization directly to reading comprehension rather than treating it as a separate, old-fashioned skill.

Invokes Daniel Willingham's cognitive-science research that skills teachers prize most -- analysis, critical thinking -- actually require extensive factual knowledge to function, undercutting the 'skills over facts' framing common in modern pedagogy.
Traces the 'memorization is drudgery' attitude back to at least 1982, showing this is a decades-old, not new, educational assumption -- and argues it was wrong from the start.
quotes: In an 1854 lecture at the University of Lille, French inventor Louis Pasteur famously said, in the fields of observation, chance favors only the prepared mind. In other words, scientific breakthroughs depend on a scientist's prior knowledge.
Sadly, very few students today memorize anything other than the multiplication table. Even forty years ago, memorization was on its way out.

In The Knowledge Deficit, E.D. Hirsch writes, The systematic acquisition of broad knowledge is precisely what it takes to become a good reader. He goes on to laud factual knowledge as well as the language it entails.

education researcher Daniel Willingham explains, research from cognitive science has shown that the sorts of skills that teachers want for students -- such as the ability to analyze and to think critically -- require extensive factual knowledge.

We are, at our core, remembering and story-making creatures, says Wilfred McClay in his American history textbook, Land of Hope. He continues, A culture without memory will necessarily be barbarous and easily tyrannized, even if it is technologically advanced.
Schools should bring back memorization. Students deserve to have rich, beautiful, informative, and culturally important knowledge in their mind's permanent collection.
